title: German present tense & word order
examples: When do I put the verb in the sentence?
What are the endings for regular verbs?
Does the word order change if I start with time?

explain.say: Today we learn about German word order in the present tense.

items: German sentences usually put the verb second.
The verb position is very important in German.
We will learn the rules for this today.

explain.say: First we look at verb endings for regular verbs.
For example the verb machen means to do or make.
Next we learn the main rule: the verb is always in the second spot.
When you start with time or manner the verb still stays in the second spot.
In real life you use this when telling someone what time you do things.

faq.q: Does the word order change if I start with a place?
faq.a: No, the verb always stays in the second position regardless of what you start with. You can start with time, manner, or place.
asks: What if I start with a place name?
Does the verb always follow the first word?

faq.q: How do I know which verb ending to use for 'you'?
faq.a: For 'du' you usually add '-st' to the verb stem. For example, 'du sprichst' for speak.
asks: Can you show me the 'du' ending again?

faq.q: Is the verb always the second word, even if there are numbers?
faq.a: Yes, the verb remains in the second position. The word order rule is very strict in German.
asks: Does the verb move if I use numbers?

faq.q: What is the difference between time and manner?
faq.a: Time tells you when something happens, like 'tomorrow'. Manner tells you how something happens, like 'quickly'.
asks: Can manner and time be swapped?

faq.q: Do I have to use the full verb form every time?
faq.a: Yes, you must conjugate the verb correctly to match the subject pronoun like 'ich' or 'er'.
asks: Do I change the verb for 'I'?
What is the correct form for 'we'?

facts: The basic word order is Subject - Verb - Object.
For 'ich' the verb ending is usually -e.
If a sentence starts with time, the verb still comes second.
The verb ending changes based on the subject pronoun.

wrong.2: This is the ending for 'du', not 'ich'.
